Unblameable
un-blām'a-bl
adj. (not liable to censure; the condition in which Christ will present His people, and the manner of a faithful ministry)
From un- and blameable, rendering Greek amomos (without spot, a sacrificial term) and amemptos (without ground of complaint). The first speaks of what a thing is; the second of what can be charged against it.

Biblical Definition

“In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight” (Colossians 1:22). The three adjectives are the goal of the reconciliation described in the verse before, and the means is named without ambiguity — the body of His flesh through death. This is not a standard set for the believer to reach but a condition Christ undertakes to produce, and the sacrificial word amomos is the one used of a lamb without blemish. Paul prays for the same thing over the Thessalonians: “To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints” (1 Thessalonians 3:13), and closes the epistle with the prayer that their whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless (1 Thessalonians 5:23) — a work he attributes to the God of peace, not to their effort. There is also a present sense, used of conduct: “Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe” (1 Thessalonians 2:10). Paul could say that of his ministry, and the claim is not sinlessness but a life against which no just charge could be laid.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unblamable as not blamable, upright, innocent, not deserving censure.

expand to see more

UNBLAMABLE, a. Not blamable; not culpable; innocent.

UNBLAMABLY, adv. In a manner not to incur blame.

BLAMELESS, a. Without fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure.

UNREPROVABLE, a. Not deserving reproof.

PRESENT, v.t. To set, place or introduce before or in the presence of a superior.

Key Scripture

Colossians 1:22 — "In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight:"

1 Thessalonians 3:13 — "To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints."

1 Thessalonians 2:10 — "Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe:"

1 Thessalonians 5:23 — "And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ."

Modern Corruption

A word describing what Christ will make of His people is read as a standard they must achieve, and assurance dies under it.

expand to see more

Colossians 1:22 is regularly preached as an exhortation — be unblameable, so that you may be presented so. The grammar is against it. Christ is the subject of the presenting, the reconciled are the object, and the instrument is the body of His flesh through death. The same pattern holds in 1 Thessalonians, where Paul does not tell them to preserve themselves blameless but prays that the God of peace would preserve them. Turn the promise into a requirement and the perfectionist and the despairing conscience both follow inevitably: one man claims he has arrived, the other concludes he never will.

The opposite error takes the imputed standing as though it made present conduct indifferent, which 1 Thessalonians 2:10 forbids by example. Paul appeals to the Thessalonians and to God as witnesses of how he behaved among them — holily, justly, unblameably. A minister able to say that is not claiming perfection; he is claiming that his life would bear inspection. The Reformed order keeps the two together in their right places: unblameable before God by the imputed righteousness of Christ, and unblameable before men by a life the Spirit is actually changing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek amomos (G299), without blemish — Colossians 1:22, Ephesians 1:4; amemptos (G273), without ground of blame — 1 Thessalonians 3:13, Philippians 3:6.

expand to see more

Greek amomos (G299) — unblemished, a sacrificial term; Colossians 1:22, Ephesians 1:4, 1 Peter 1:19 of the Lamb Himself.

Greek amemptos (G273) — blameless, without just charge; 1 Thessalonians 3:13, and Philippians 3:6 of Paul's former standing in the law.

Greek anegkletos (G410) — unreproveable, unaccused; Colossians 1:22, and required of elders and deacons in 1 Timothy 3:10, Titus 1:6.

Greek paristemi (G3936) — to present, to set beside; Colossians 1:22, of what Christ does with His people.

1 Peter 1:19 shows why the sacrificial word fits: a lamb without blemish and without spot, and His people are made like Him.

Usage

"“To present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight” — He presents; we are presented."

"“Stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness” — a prayer, not a demand."

"“How holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves” — a life that bore inspection."
